metadata.title: Prioritisation of ophthalmic procedures
metadata.summary: This guidance groups ophthalmic procedures into priority levels according to how soon they are needed and the potential harm from delay. It is intended to help UK ophthalmic services allocate restricted capacity during recovery from the SARS-CoV-2 pandemic while reviewing patients whose treatment is deferred. The list covers major procedures but is not exhaustive; decisions must account for individual circumstances and clinical risk.

care_settings: ophthalmic departments providing emergency, urgent and elective procedures
target_population: Patients whose ophthalmic treatment has been deferred

Eye removal is prioritised within 72 hours when there is a serious risk to systemic health, such as sepsis.

recommendations.statement: Take each patient's circumstances, clinical risk, urgency and needs into account when deciding when to perform an ophthalmic procedure.
recommendations.context: The priority levels provide guidance rather than replacing decisions about individual patients.
recommendations.source_heading: 1 Introduction

recommendations.statement: Services may adapt the procedure list into a prioritisation system suited to the healthcare needs of their local population and the services they provide.
recommendations.source_heading: 1 Introduction

recommendations.statement: Keep a clear record of every decision to defer treatment for an individual patient or a group of patients.
recommendations.context: Reduced ophthalmic service capacity during the SARS-CoV-2 pandemic.
recommendations.rationale: Patients must not be lost to follow-up while services are reduced or recovering.
recommendations.source_heading: 2 Risk of delaying procedures and loss to follow up

recommendations.statement: Review patients whose treatment has been deferred in a coordinated manner at regular intervals to check that the delay is not causing harm.
recommendations.source_heading: 2 Risk of delaying procedures and loss to follow up

recommendations.statement: Assess the risk of harm from postponement whenever treatment is deferred for a patient or a group of patients.
recommendations.source_heading: 2 Risk of delaying procedures and loss to follow up

recommendations.statement: Allow ophthalmologists to assign a patient's risk category using clinical judgement when individual circumstances differ from the listed category.
recommendations.context: The procedure risk categories do not necessarily apply to every patient.

special_populations.considerations: The paediatric priority categories also include applicable adult procedures. Additional time-sensitive circumstances include conditions that may threaten sight, severe ptosis associated with actual or likely amblyopia, and glaucoma requiring drainage surgery.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Within 72 hours: retinal laser or intravitreal injections for retinopathy of prematurity, and examination under anaesthesia for potentially sight-threatening disease. Within 4 weeks: congenital cataract surgery, superficial keratectomy for atopic plaque, surgery or plaque for retinoblastoma, and glaucoma drainage surgery (within 2 weeks). Within 3-4 months: retinal laser, cryotherapy or intravitreal injections for retinal vascular conditions; removal of loose corneal sutures; and YAG laser or surgical capsulotomy for visual axis opacity following congenital cataract surgery. The guide also places surgery for severe ptosis with actual or likely amblyopia and corneal surgery for congenital corneal opacity within 4 weeks, and surgery for paediatric orbital floor fracture with muscle entrapment within 72 hours.

document_sections.heading: 1 Introduction
document_sections.content: The SARS-CoV-2 pandemic substantially changed healthcare provision in the UK, and infection-control measures reduced ophthalmic services. This guidance helps departments prioritise eye surgery as services reopen, when capacity may remain limited even as more moderately urgent and elective care resumes. It covers the main ophthalmic procedures but is not exhaustive and does not address complex, uncommon or specialised procedures in detail. Each decision must account for the patient's circumstances, risk, urgency and needs; services may adapt the priorities to their local population and available services. The introductory priority list places emergency procedures at Level 1, within 24 hours; urgent procedures at Level 2, within 72 hours; Level 3 procedures within 4 weeks; Level 4 procedures within 3 months; and Level 5 procedures after more than 3 months. These intervals reflect usual practice and the greater risk of an adverse outcome when a condition progresses or worsens during a delay.

document_sections.heading: 2 Risk of delaying procedures and loss to follow up
document_sections.content: The SARS-CoV-2 pandemic has placed ophthalmic services under severe strain. Services must avoid losing patients to follow-up during reduced activity and recovery. Some treatments for lower-risk conditions will need to be deferred so that patients at greater risk of visual loss can be seen. Decisions to defer treatment for an individual or group must be clearly recorded and must assess the risk of harm from delay. Deferred patients require coordinated review at regular intervals to check that the postponement is not causing harm. The risk table identifies High Risk, Medium Risk and Low Risk categories for harm associated with deferral. A patient's circumstances may place them in a different category from the one indicated for a procedure, so ophthalmologists must retain discretion to assign risk using clinical judgement. Some procedures belong to more than one subspecialty but appear only once in the subsequent tables for concision.

document_sections.heading: 3 Level 1: Emergency procedures needed within 24 hours
document_sections.content: The table places procedures requiring intervention within 24 hours across vitreoretinal care, adnexal care, trauma, ocular oncology and paediatrics. It includes vitreous biopsy with antibiotic injections for suspected infectious endophthalmitis; emergency eye surgery for trauma threatening sight or causing disfigurement, such as penetrating injury, globe rupture, orbital haemorrhage or lid laceration; and removal of a Ruthenium-plaque. The adnexal entry refers to the trauma category, while the paediatric category refers to applicable adult procedures.

document_sections.heading: 4 Level 2: Urgent procedures needed within 72 hours
document_sections.content: The table identifies procedures needed within 72 hours in vitreoretinal, medical retina, adnexal, trauma, glaucoma, external eye, neuro-ophthalmic and paediatric care. Vitreoretinal entries cover laser for retinal tears, vitrectomy after a lens nucleus drops during cataract surgery, and surgery for acute rhegmatogenous retinal detachment when the macula remains attached or has recently detached. Other entries include periocular or intravitreal steroids for inflammatory eye disease; decompression or debulking for sight-threatening orbital disease; orbital abscess drainage; and eye removal when systemic health faces a serious risk, such as sepsis. Trauma procedures address intraocular or very deep /full thickness corneal foreign bodies and paediatric orbital floor fractures with muscle entrapment. Glaucoma procedures include drainage surgery or diode laser for some secondary glaucoma with very high pressure and likely imminent visual loss, drainage surgery for acute glaucoma unresponsive to medical treatment and laser, and Laser PI for acute glaucoma. External eye procedures include emergency corneal transplantation or glueing and amniotic membrane grafting for imminently sight-threatening disease, including severe chemical burns or Stevens Johnson/toxic epidermal necrolysis. The table also includes temporal artery biopsy, retinal laser or intravitreal injections for retinopathy of prematurity, and examination under anaesthesia for potentially sight-threatening disease.

document_sections.heading: 5 Level 3: Procedures needed within 4 weeks
document_sections.content: The table groups procedures needed within 4 weeks by subspecialty. Vitreoretinal procedures include repeat surgery for retinal detachment, vitrectomy for a dislocated lens implant when the other eye has poor vision, vitrectomy for acute vitreous haemorrhage with a suspected retinal break / unknown cause, and vitrectomy for retinal detachment with the macula off for more than 2 weeks. Medical retina procedures include intravitreal injections for wet age related macular degeneration <2 weeks, laser for active or progressive retinal neovascularization, and periocular or intravitreal steroid injection for macular oedema. Adnexal surgery addresses ocular-surface protection, eyelid cancers, orbital tumours and severe ptosis in children who are developing or likely to develop amblyopia. Glaucoma entries cover cataract surgery for imminently sight-threatening angle closure glaucoma, drainage surgery for sight-threatening very high IOP or a very high risk of vision loss in an only eye, and intravitreal injection and/or retinal laser for iris/angle rubeosis. Other entries include intumescent cataract extraction; superficial keratectomy for atopic plaque in children; amniotic membrane grafting for a surface ulcer that does not heal; and surgery for congenital corneal opacity. Ocular oncology entries cover surgical, laser or radiation treatment of ocular and ocular-surface tumours, enucleation for advanced melanoma or other malignancies, intravitreal injections for radiation maculopathy and/or ocular tumours, and PDT or external beam radiotherapy for sight-threatening ocular metastases. Paediatric entries also include congenital cataract surgery, glaucoma drainage surgery within 2 weeks, and surgery or plaque treatment for retinoblastoma.

document_sections.heading: 6 Level 4: Procedures needed within 3-4 months
document_sections.content: The table places selected vitreoretinal, medical retina, adnexal, glaucoma, cataract, external eye and paediatric procedures within 3-4 months. Vitreoretinal entries include some macular-hole surgery, vitrectomy for vitreous haemorrhage or tractional retinal detachment, and vitrectomy to remove silicone oil when complications occur. Medical retina entries include intravitreal injections for diabetic macular oedema or retinal vein occlusion, macular laser for diabetic macular oedema or branch retinal vein occlusion, and photodynamic laser surgery for central serous chorioretinopathy. Adnexal entries include lacrimal surgery for a large mucocele, correction of entropion or ectropion when the ocular surface is damaged, toxin injections for blepharospasm that disables vision, and eye removal when neither malignancy nor an urgent systemic-health threat is present. Glaucoma entries comprise drainage surgery and Selective laser trabeculoplasty laser. Cataract surgery or YAG laser capsulotomy is included when binocular vision is <6/60 or disability is severe, such as inability to work, or when it limits management of another sight-threatening condition. Other entries include cross-linking for rapidly progressive keratoconus or keratoconus with a very thin cornea; retinal laser, cryotherapy or intravitreal injections for paediatric retinal vascular conditions; removal of loose corneal sutures in children; and YAG laser or surgical capsulotomy for visual-axis opacity after congenital cataract surgery.

document_sections.heading: 7 Level 5: Procedures which can be carried out in more than 3-4 months
document_sections.content: The table identifies procedures that may take place after more than 3-4 months. Vitreoretinal entries include vitrectomy for macular epiretinal membrane, silicone oil removal without complications and other routine surgery. Medical retina includes retinal laser for severe pre-proliferative diabetic retinopathy. Adnexal entries include Dacrocystorhinostomy and other routine surgery. Cataract entries include YAG laser capsulotomy, cataract surgery for significant binocular visual reduction and routine cataract surgery. Other entries cover PI laser for narrow angles; cross-linking for progressive keratoconus and other routine external eye surgery; reconstruction or debulking of benign tumours and other routine ocular oncology surgery; and strabismus surgery for restoration of visual function, other strabismus surgery and other routine paediatric or strabismus procedures.
